Part 1 opens briefly on credibility: the three operations that go under the word 'replication', and the five Multi100 analysts of one claim, who disagreed but whose disagreement could be diagnosed afterwards because every one of them shipped a document that somebody else could run. The rest of the part lays out the toolchain that makes that kind of checking possible. The hands-on work comes at the end and runs into the first break, so that if your machine gives trouble you miss none of the talk. The part takes ninety minutes.

## 1. The plan of the day

**On the slides.** The facilitator sets out the plan of the day and its two kinds of aim, what you will understand and what you will be able to do, and the slides say what you do not need. Open the browser lab in a tab and leave it to load while the facilitator talks, and if you installed the workspace, open its folder in your IDE as well.

[Open the browser lab](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

## 2. The three Rs

**On the slides.** A matrix of data against analysis separates reproduction, robustness and replication. The slides then turn to repeatability and credibility, a quick check on the matrix in peer review, and the practices of open research.

## 3. Multi100 from the inside

**On the slides.** The slides show what an analyst received, the paper in brief, the two Multi100 tasks and the common scale on which the results of the five were put, and a forest plot of the five analysts of the claim. The slides end on the software and the document format that each analyst used, which is where the toolchain starts.

## 4. The toolchain

**On the slides.** The toolchain is taken apart layer by layer, from open-source software and the map of the tools to programming languages, editors and IDEs. The slides go on to plain-text file formats and what happens when a document renders, and to the package layer, and the run ends on version control, where data and code are archived, and licences.

To go further: [Positron and other IDEs](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/ide.html), [Quarto documents](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/quarto.html) and [Git and GitHub](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/git-github.html) on the AR4DS site.

## 5. The browser lab and the workspace

**On the slides.** The slides compare the browser lab with the workspace and say what the tools cannot do.

## 6. Task 1 – The setup check

[Open the browser lab at Task 1](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd#task-1-setup){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

In the browser lab, wait for the R engine, run the three setup cells, and confirm that the second reports 270 rows, 27 countries and 10 years. If you have installed the workspace, open its folder in your IDE instead and run `source("R/check_setup.R")` until it reports no failure. The aim is to reach the point at which a line of R runs and the panel is in front of you, and if you need more time, carry on into the break.

**By the end of the part** R runs on your machine, you can tell apart the three operations that go under the word 'replication', and you can place any tool that someone names on the map of the toolchain.
